description: Baudelaire draws beauty out of evil and out of everyday life in Paris. Condemned in 1857, Les Fleurs du Mal founded modern poetry.

hero.hook: Six censored poems, one conviction, and the birth of modern poetry.

blocks.text: In **1857**, **Charles Baudelaire** published **Les Fleurs du Mal** (*The Flowers of Evil*). The collection marked a turning point in the history of poetry. Until then, **[[Romanticism]]** had ruled: poets idealized nature and noble feelings. Baudelaire did something else. He wrote about ugliness, sin, the city, and dread.

The book caused a scandal. A court condemned it for “outrage to public morals.” Yet Baudelaire was defending a strong idea: beauty can be drawn out of what shocks or disgusts. He compared the poet to an alchemist. Where others saw only mud, he looked for gold.

**Charles Baudelaire** embodied the **poète maudit**, the cursed poet: a writer on the margins, out of step with his own age. His hard life fed his work. He loved elegance and refinement, what the period called **dandyism**, but he also knew ruin and debt.

His father died when he was **6**, and he fought with his stepfather, General **Aupick**, who controlled part of his fortune. He loved **Jeanne Duval**, an actress and singer. Their relationship was passionate and stormy. She inspired several poems in the collection.

blocks.caption: Charles Baudelaire: elegance, pain, and modernity

blocks.text: Six poems were banned in 1857 and only officially cleared in 1949, 92 years after the verdict.

In **1857**, the same year as the trial of **[[Madame Bovary]]**, **Les Fleurs du Mal** went to court too. Flaubert and Baudelaire were both prosecuted for immorality. Baudelaire was also translating **Edgar Allan Poe**, the American master of the uncanny. He called Poe a “soul brother,” sharing his taste for the macabre.

The book is not just a pile of poems. Baudelaire traced a progression through it. The first big section, **“Spleen and Ideal,”** sets two states against each other. **Spleen**, an English word he carried into French, means a deep boredom, a sadness with no cause. The **ideal** is the thirst for height and pure beauty.

In **“The Albatross,”** the poet compares himself to that seabird. In flight it is magnificent. On the deck of a ship it turns clumsy and ridiculous. The image sums up the loneliness of the artist nobody understands.

blocks.caption: Paris by night in the 1850s: the setting of Baudelairean spleen

blocks.text: **“Parisian Scenes”** turns the city into an inner landscape. Streets, crowds, and passing women mirror the poet's moods. Under **[[Baron Haussmann]]**, Paris was being rebuilt: wide boulevards, new apartment blocks. Baudelaire wandered through it as a **flâneur**, a stroller who watches the city with no fixed aim. The sections “Wine,” “Flowers of Evil,” and “Revolt” try out ways of escape before the book closes on “Death.”

Baudelaire had mastered the classical forms. He often wrote in the **sonnet**, a poem of 14 lines, or in the **alexandrine**, a line of 12 syllables. Into those old forms he brought a new vision. His poem **“Correspondences”** describes nature as a temple where scents, colors, and sounds answer one another.
Nature is a temple where living pillars / Sometimes let slip confused words.

Here he develops the idea of **synesthesia**: the senses blend into each other. You can “smell” a color or “see” a perfume. The world becomes a web of signs for the poet to decipher. This poetics is the road that leads to **[[Symbolism and Baudelaire's legacy]]**, carried on later by Verlaine and Mallarmé.
The whole project fits into one famous line: “You gave me your mud and I made gold of it.” Baudelaire never denies evil or ugliness. He turns them into material for art.

For Baudelaire, **[[Modernity]]** means catching what passes: city life, the fleeting, the everyday. But he was also looking for what lasts. The modern poet studies his own time instead of running from it.

This attention to the city prepared the **[[prose poem]]**, a poetic text with no meter and no rhyme. Baudelaire developed it in **[[Le Spleen de Paris]]**, a posthumous collection of short prose poems about Paris.

events.detail: Verlaine, Mallarmé, and the poetry of the 20th century.
events.title: Symbolism

blocks.text: Baudelaire also redefined the role of the poet. In Hugo, the poet still guides the nation. In Baudelaire, he becomes an outsider who sees what society would rather hide. **Les Fleurs du Mal** shocked readers first, then became a reference point for the whole century that followed.

**Les Fleurs du Mal** changed poetry by pulling beauty out of evil and out of daily life in the city. The collection founded **[[Modernity]]** in verse and opened the road to **[[Symbolism and Baudelaire's legacy]]**, despite a ban that lasted nearly a century.
